newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabweans go to work despite strike call.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabweans go to work despite strike call.

text.p: Zimbabwean workers turned up for duty as usual on Tuesday despite calls by trade unions for a national stoppage in support of striking nurses and doctors.

Early on Tuesday, the government deployed police and secret agents in major centres in a measure Acting Public Service, Labour and Social Welfare Minister Nathan Shamuyarira said was aimed at protecting workers from being intimidated by union leaders to join the strike.
A union leader said the workers had not heeded the strike calls, seen as a political challenge by the embattled government of President Robert Mugabe, because they were made late.

"We made a decision and announced it too late in the day, that's why people are at work. We all now realise we needed more time to organise it...and we are doing that now," Morgan Tsvangirayi, secretary-general of the Zimbabwe Congress of Trade Unions (ZCTU), told Reuters.
"If need be, we are going to be in a long fight to open government's ears," he added, accusing the dominant state media of blocking out its message.

The ZCTU represents about 200,000 of Zimbabwe's two million workers in the key farming, tourism, banking, energy, mining and manufacturing sectors. Its calls are usually heeded by a majority, including the non-unionised workers.

It called a two-day nationwide strike on Monday evening, hours after armed riot-control police used teargas and batons to break up a planned mass demonstration organised by the unions, churches and human rights groups to press the government to resolve the three-week-old strike by nurses and doctors.
The strike by medical workers is over demands for higher wages and better working conditions. A majority of the 180,000 civil servants staged a three-week strike over pay last month.

The government ended the first strike by awarding the workers 20 percent salary rises, and promises of talks on their demands for wage increases of up to 60 percent which the current strikers say it has failed to keep.
The government says it needs time to look at the issues.
Mugabe's 16-year-old government, defying overwhelming public pressure, vows it will not back down and denies charges it has become insolent and arrogant.
Mugabe left for Rome late on Monday to attend the World Food Summit, drawing criticism from Tsvangirayi who told state television on Monday that he should have stayed home to resolve the strike.
Shamuyarira hit back, saying Mugabe's presence at the summit was crucial because Zimbabwe was agriculture-based.
"He has to be there...and it's not for some irresponsible trade union leader to tell him how he uses his time," he said.
The government accuses its political opponents, notably veteran opposition leader Ndabaningi Sithole, of using the strikers to undermine its authority. He denies the charge.
"All the known opposition parties are supporting and helping to organise it. The organisers are seeking a political objective," Shamuyarira said on Monday.
The nurses' and doctors' strike has led to the closure of Zimbabwe's two largest hospitals and relatives say many patients have died due to lack of treatment.
Union officials say 10,000 of 14,000 nurses employed in state hospitals and 500 of 800 doctors are on strike, but the government says only 1,000 nurses and 100 doctors were involved.
